name: Aaron Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to your employer, government or AI companies. Your answers are confidential. Aaron, what does a usual day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We collect the permit at the depot, load fittings in the van and spend most of the day replacing damaged line parts or putting up a new connection. I like a repair that is finished properly before we leave. What wears me out is driving back for a part the drawing got wrong, then explaining the delay to a screen.

say: I would say a quicker **permit filing** is useful if repair safety stays clear.
I would tell colleagues the **line test** still needs a person at the pole.
think: I do not use **AI tools**, and small software changes do not fix our tight household budget.
A missed **standby payment** can push school costs onto a card.
do: Keep taking **repair shifts** and weekend standby when available.
Cancel the **sports subscription** this month to cover the electricity bill.
feel: I feel **settled at work** but squeezed by ordinary bills.
S0.quote: The quiet version sounds almost like today, and today is already a little tight.
fieldNote: Aaron stays with **familiar permit checks** and asks dispatch directly when details are unclear; he has never used AI tools.
His **thin cushion** is already visible in school shoes bought on a card after a missed callout.

steps.text: Continue regular line repairs and take offered weekend standby
Cancel the sports subscription to cover the electricity bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the men in the van that a computer filing the permit faster is fine by me. The line still has to be made dead and tested before anyone lifts a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not used these AI things myself. My worry is simpler: we have a mortgage, two children and less than a month put aside, so a week without callouts already hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my regular repair shifts and take the weekend standby rota when it is offered. This month my partner and I would cancel the sports subscription and put that money toward the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about the job but stretched at home. The quiet version sounds almost like today, and today is already a little tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a missed callout mean recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In August another crew got the Saturday fault and I had counted on that pay for school shoes. We bought the shoes on a card and cleared it the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new filing tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the permit arrives on my phone, I will read it as I do now. I would rather ask dispatch about a missing detail than guess what the software meant.

say: I would accept **faster schedules** if dispatch remains reachable for faulty drawings.
I would insist **repair times** be based on real site work.
think: Office staff may shrink first, but shorter targets could take away my **extra shift**.
I would rather show **site errors** than argue about software I have not used.
do: Stay on the **line crew** and record wrong locations or missing parts.
Bring the **error notebook** to the supervisor in the first rollout year.
feel: I feel **irritated** by rushed targets and worried about overtime.
S1.quote: I can live with a changed form if it does not become a smaller wage packet.
fieldNote: Aaron focuses on **overtime and site errors**, rather than learning the new planning software himself.
His first instinct is a **supervisor meeting** with a notebook; union help is a conditional next step if the roster changes.

steps.text: Continue paid line crew shifts during the planning rollout
Ask the union representative to join if the roster changes despite site evidence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can try a faster schedule, provided they still answer the phone when a crew finds a bad drawing. I do not want a screen telling me a damaged bracket is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office jobs sound more exposed than ours, because writing and buying can be done on a screen. Still, if managers set shorter repair times from computer plans, they may stop offering the extra shift I rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the line crew and write down any work orders with the wrong location or part. In the first year I would take that notebook to the supervisor and ask for repair times to be set from actual jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel irritated at the thought of being rushed, and worried about the extra hours. I can live with a changed form if it does not become a smaller wage packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is an example of a bad drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job on Mill Road was marked as a pole replacement, but the old base was sound and the bracket was split. We lost an hour getting the correct part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask a union representative to join the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first show the supervisor the notebook. If the roster changed despite that evidence, I would ask the union representative to come with me.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from robots reaching field repairs around 2031.
I would demand a **live robot trial** before any reduction in line crews.
think: I will be **48** when robots arrive and have few nearby line jobs.
Our **mortgage and food** cost more than the savings we have for one month.
do: Keep taking **paid shifts** through the first year after 2028.
Drop the **rented cabin** and ask for written robot trial rules.
feel: I feel **anxious** about 2031, while still expecting wages in 2028.
S2.quote: I would not walk away from a wage in 2028.
fieldNote: Aaron distinguishes **office AI** from the later field robots and expects to keep paid callouts in the interim.
His concrete response is to protect **mortgage cash** by dropping a cabin rental; training requires paid hours and a vacancy.

steps.text: Keep taking offered paid line callouts through the first 2028 AI year
Cancel the rented holiday cabin to keep mortgage cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that full thinking AI in 2028 does not make a line safe to touch. The robots around 2031 are the part that could replace our field shifts, and I would want to see a live trial before staffing changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when robots can do the line work. There are few other line jobs close by, and our savings would not pay even one month of mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep every paid shift I can and ask the supervisor for the company rules on robot trials. In the first year after 2028 I would take the callouts still offered and cut the family holiday budget in half while we see whether field staffing really changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the 2031 date, but I would not walk away from a wage in 2028. My partner and I would talk after the children sleep, because I do not want them planning around a job loss that has not happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the holiday would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep a few days visiting my partner's sister and drop the rented cabin. The cabin deposit is money we could need for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course right away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the company paid the hours and showed me a real field vacancy at the end. I have never used AI tools, and a course with no job attached would be a bad bet for us.

say: I would ask for **bad-weather trials** before judging field robots safe.
I would note **2031 AI** comes before hands-on machines around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still owe on the mortgage and need a full wage.
I might take **field maintenance** if the vacancy and comparable pay are real.
do: Request **trial dates** each year and continue paid line repairs in 2031.
Watch a paid **robot trial** and apply for a comparable field maintenance opening.
feel: I feel **less hurried** but suspicious of a career plan built on demonstrations.
S3.quote: I do not want to spend evenings teaching myself from a screen while the family waits for me.
fieldNote: Aaron wants **observed bad-weather performance** before accepting claims about robots, consistent with his preference for familiar methods.
He would consider **paid hands-on instruction** and a field vacancy, but refuses to count on retirement at 51.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts in the first 2031 AI year
Apply for a comparable company field maintenance vacancy if offered
Learn robot controls beside an experienced operator on paid shifts if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough for the company to show us what a robot can do on a bad line, not just in a clear yard. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and the hands-on machine comes around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 at the second. One child might be leaving school by then, but I cannot assume the mortgage is finished or that I can retire at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the supervisor to put field trial dates on the staff noticeboard each year. In 2031 I would stay on repairs, ask to watch a robot trial on paid time, and apply for a company field maintenance vacancy if it offered similar pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little less hurried than in the two-year case. I still do not like planning a new career from a machine demonstration that has not happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the fittings and can spot when a repair has been done badly. A field maintenance job might use that, but I would check the wage before filling in an application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the robot controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company put me beside an experienced operator on paid shifts, I would try. I do not want to spend evenings teaching myself from a screen while the family waits for me.

say: I would ask for **actual crew hours** from robot pilots each year.
I would separate **2036 office AI** from robots reaching line repairs around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or retirement is funded.
An **office planning role** would be vulnerable once full AI handles the plans.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** and review annual crew hours with my partner.
Pay an extra **thirty** against the mortgage when overtime is reliable.
feel: I feel **steady for now** and cautious about the later robot date.
S4.quote: The children could be grown, but I will not treat that as money in the bank or assume our mortgage is gone.
fieldNote: Aaron expects continued **paid physical work** over the near term and wants observed crew hours before making a move.
He sees **mortgage payments** as ongoing and treats a maintenance application as conditional on falling field hours and comparable pay.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Pay thirty extra against mortgage principal when overtime is reliable
Apply for a comparable maintenance post if field hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a decade is time for facts, not a promise about a machine we have not seen. AI could change the office in 2036, while robots may reach line repair around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the AI date and 56 when robots arrive. The children could be grown, but I will not treat that as money in the bank or assume our mortgage is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line job now and ask the supervisor each year how many hours crews actually worked after any pilot. In 2036 I would stay on paid repairs, compare the figures with my partner, and pay an extra thirty toward the mortgage in months when overtime is reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady over the next few years because the pole work is still there. The robot date is far enough away to check the facts, though I would not promise an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for a different job by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the field hours were dropping and a comparable maintenance post was advertised, I would apply. I would not move to an office planning job when full AI can handle the plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that I stayed with a trade I knew while I watched the numbers. I would also say the mortgage took longer than I expected when they were small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots could reach the line around 2031 and that is a short run for a family with almost no savings. Real trials in bad weather, paid training linked to a field vacancy and straight answers about crew hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will still pay us while we learn. A promise of training is thin comfort if the mortgage is due before the course ends.

headlineQuote: A promise of training is thin comfort if the mortgage is due before the course ends.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He avoids **AI tools** and trusts permits, field checks and repairs he can inspect himself.
His **thin savings** and lower pay make standby hours important even if AI barely changes his trade.
Across the scenarios he wants **real trials**, paid shifts and comparable field vacancies before risking a job change.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** gives his household little time before robots could reach line repairs around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Real **bad-weather trials**, paid training tied to a vacancy and clear crew-hour figures would help him plan.
